media.title: Weight Check
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Weight Check

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S1.T1.C2.2D1
- Tool type: Exploration (the free first try: after the hook video, before the concept video)
- Textbook source: Weight and Capacity, the opener task "Check! Check!" on Anu's list: iron almirah 40 g, bed 60 kg, rice bag 5 kg, sofa 30 g, bucket 1 kg 800 g, water bottle 650 g, refrigerator 50 g. The other things and numbers in Activities 1 to 4 are practice values (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student sees that a heavy thing cannot weigh only a few grams, by putting it against a 1 kg block (1,000 g) and reading the unit on its tag.
- Out of scope: changing units in sums, reading scales, mixed weights, stating the rule in words (the concept video that follows does that).

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- Anu's room as a photo-style 3D scene: tiled floor, a window with soft daylight, the refrigerator and the iron almirah against the wall, a bed and a sofa at the sides, a bucket and a water bottle on the floor. Anu (flat drawing, holding her list) stands in a corner.
- In the middle of the floor stands a two-pan steel balance, about 40% of the stage width. The right pan holds a steel block painted "1 kg (1,000 g)". The left pan is empty and level. The iron almirah cut-out waits in a glowing circle beside the left pan with a paper tag tied to it: "40 g".
- Instruction line: "Anu says this almirah weighs 40 g. Which side will go down?" The child is invited to tap one of two big arrows under the balance: "Almirah side" or "Block side".

2. Scene and Objects
- Things not in use sit on a low wooden shelf along the front edge of the stage, each cut-out about 14% of the stage width, each with a paper tag on a string. Only the things of the current activity are on the shelf.
- The balance: the pans dip about one pan-height when one side is heavier and stay level when the sides are about equal. The 1 kg block never leaves the right pan.
- Things (photo cut-outs): the seven things of Anu's list; a pencil, a school bag, a brick; a banana, a bicycle; a lemon, a sack of wheat, a pencil box, a gas cylinder.
- Two wicker bins at the front corners, each about 15% of the stage width: "g" and "kg" in Activity 4; "Looks right" and "Does not look right" in the star challenge.
- Under the balance: the guess arrows and one plain sentence line. Goal chip at the top left.

3. Main Interaction
- Guess arrows (Activities 1 and 2): tap one, named for the thing and the block, for example "Pencil side" and "Block side". The pan stays locked until one is tapped.
- Drag a thing onto the left pan, one at a time (a second drop sends the first back to the shelf). The pans swing for about a second and a sentence appears: "The thing is heavier than the 1 kg block.", "The thing is lighter than the 1 kg block." or, for the bucket and the water bottle, "The thing is close to the 1 kg block. Decide with the tag."
- A tag can be dragged only after its thing has been on the balance once. A tag dropped in a bin snaps in; dragging it out returns it. In Activity 3 the child taps one of two tags.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset", and one main button "Check" that turns into "Next" when the step is right. Wrong drops slide back. Retry is always free.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Anu says this almirah weighs 40 g. Which side will go down?" Goal chip: "Almirah or 1 kg block?" Setup: the almirah with its tag "40 g". Guess: the child taps "Almirah side" or "Block side", then drags the almirah onto the left pan. Result: the almirah side drops, the chip turns green with a bounce, and the tag "40 g" and the block label glow together; strip "The almirah is much heavier than the 1 kg block, which is 1,000 g. The tag says only 40 g." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Put the pencil, the school bag and the brick on the balance, one at a time." Goal chip: "Heavier or lighter than 1 kg?" Setup: three cut-outs with "?" tags. For each, the child taps a guess arrow ("Thing side" or "Block side"), then drops it. Results: pencil, the block side goes down: "The pencil is lighter than 1 kg, so it weighs less than 1,000 g." School bag and brick, the thing side goes down: "The school bag is heavier than 1 kg, so it weighs more than 1,000 g." and the same for the brick. Help: guided, "1,000 g" stays large.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "Pick the tag that fits." Goal chip: "Which tag fits?" Setup: a banana with two tags "150 g" and "150 kg", then a bicycle with "12 g" and "12 kg". Guess: the child taps a tag; nothing moves until Check. Result: the fitting tag ties on and the other drops. Banana: "A banana is lighter than 1 kg, so 150 g fits. 150 kg is 150,000 g, far too heavy for a banana." Bicycle: "A bicycle is heavier than 1 kg, so 12 kg fits. 12 g is far too light for a bicycle." Help: guided, the balance and block stay on screen.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Is it g or kg? Drop each card in the right bin." Goal chip: "g or kg?" Setup: four cards with a number and no unit: lemon "80", sack of wheat "25", pencil box "200", gas cylinder "14"; bins "g" and "kg". Guess: the child drops each card in a bin, then presses Check. Result: "A lemon and a pencil box are lighter than 1 kg, so they are in g. A sack of wheat and a gas cylinder are heavier than 1 kg, so they are in kg." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent), the book's task: "Anu has recorded the weights of the items in her house. Check if she has recorded them correctly by putting a tick against them if they look correct." Goal chip: "Tick the weights that look right". Setup: the seven things with tags: Iron Almirah 40 g, Bed 60 kg, Rice Bag 5 kg, Sofa 30 g, Bucket 1 kg 800 g, Water Bottle 650 g, Refrigerator 50 g. The child weighs each against the block and drops its tag in "Looks right" or "Does not look right" (the bin is the guess). Result after Check: the almirah, sofa and refrigerator tags must be in "Does not look right": "The almirah, the sofa and the refrigerator are much heavier than 1 kg. Their tags say 40 g, 30 g and 50 g, all far less than 1,000 g." The other four may go in either bin, each with a calm note such as "A bed is much heavier than 1 kg. 60 kg is far more than 1,000 g, so it can fit." Then: "Sample answer: the bed, the rice bag, the bucket and the water bottle look right. Your answer may differ for the bed, the bucket and the bottle." Help: independent.

5. Mathematical Understanding
- The balance shows a thing is heavier or lighter than 1 kg, which is 1,000 g. A weight in g far below 1,000 g belongs to a light thing; a heavy thing needs 1 kg or more.
- The number alone does not tell the weight: 150 g and 150 kg are very different. The rule is not stated in words here; the concept video names it.

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick, the main button becomes "Next".
- Guesses the wrong side, for example "Thing side" for the pencil -> "The block side went down. A pencil is lighter than the 1 kg block." The thing glows.
- Taps "150 kg" for the banana -> "150 kg is 150,000 g. Is a banana that heavy?" Taps "12 g" for the bicycle -> "12 g is far less than 1,000 g. Is a bicycle lighter than the 1 kg block?" The block label pulses.
- Puts a card in the wrong bin, for example the lemon in "kg" -> "A lemon is lighter than the 1 kg block. Try g." A heavy thing in "g" gets "A sack of wheat is heavier than the 1 kg block. Try kg." The right bin pulses.
- Puts the almirah, sofa or refrigerator tag in "Looks right" -> "The balance says it is much heavier than 1 kg, but the tag says 40 g (30 g, 50 g). That is far less than 1,000 g. Look again at the tag." The tag and the block label pulse.
- Calls 60 kg "too big" for a bed -> "60 kg is 60,000 g. A bed is much heavier than 1 kg, so a big weight can fit." A calm note, never a red strip, because the bed is open to judgement.
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Which side of the balance goes down? Is the thing heavier than the 1 kg block?" (2) visual clue: the block and its "1,000 g" label pulse and the unit letters on the tag glow. (3) almost the answer: "The almirah is much heavier than 1 kg, so it should weigh more than 1,000 g. Does the tag say more than 1,000 g?" and the right bin glows softly.
- Edge cases: the bucket and the water bottle make the balance almost level, so the tool says "close to the 1 kg block" and never calls them wrong. A tag dropped before its thing was weighed bounces back with "Put the thing on the balance first."

7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when all seven tags are in bins and the almirah, sofa and refrigerator tags are in "Does not look right".
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "A heavy thing weighs more than 1 kg, which is 1,000 g." "Read the unit as well as the number: g is for light things and kg is for heavy things." Think and talk: "Anu's sofa tag says 30 g. What would you tell her?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: Anu's room as a photo-style 3D scene; a two-pan steel balance; a steel 1 kg block with a painted label; cut-outs of an iron almirah, bed, cloth rice bag, sofa, plastic bucket, water bottle, refrigerator, pencil, school bag, brick, banana, bicycle, lemon, sack of wheat, pencil box and gas cylinder; two wicker bins; paper tags; Anu as a flat drawing. Code-drawn: pan tilt, tags, arrows, chips. Simple English.

tool_config.idea: Decide whether a recorded weight looks right for a thing by putting the thing on a balance against a 1 kg block and reading the unit: a thing heavier than the block must weigh 1 kg or more, which is 1,000 g or more, so a weight like 40 g cannot be right for it. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names the idea.
tool_config.title: Weight Check
tool_config.screen: Anu's room from your maths book, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A two pan balance stands on the floor in the middle of the room and is the largest thing on screen. The right pan always holds a 1 kg block labelled 1 kg = 1,000 g. Around the balance, along the wall, are picture cards of the seven things on Anu's list: an iron almirah, a bed, a rice bag, a sofa, a bucket, a water bottle and a refrigerator, each with a tag showing the weight Anu wrote (40 g, 60 kg, 5 kg, 30 g, 1 kg 800 g, 650 g, 50 g). Two bins stand at the front, Looks right and Does not look right. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a picture card onto the left pan (the balance tips and a plain sentence under it says whether the thing is heavier than, lighter than or about the same as 1 kg); drag the card's tag into a bin; for practice cards, tap one of two tags to choose the fitting unit, for example 6 g or 6 kg; Check, Hint, Retry (clears the balance and the bins for this card), Reset (returns all cards), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the balance tilt with its sentence, a counter of cards placed, and a card number out of 5.
feedback: When a card goes on the pan the balance tips and the sentence says so, for example: The almirah is much heavier than the 1 kg block. For the borderline things (bucket, bottle) it says: Close to the block. Decide with the tag.

A tag dropped in a bin is read against the block, for example: The tag says 40 g. 40 g is less than 1 kg, which is 1,000 g, but the almirah is much heavier than 1 kg. Look again at the tag. The tool never calls a borderline thing wrong.
A unit tag that does not fit slides back with a clue, for example: 6 kg is 6,000 g. Is a pencil that heavy?
A card in the right bin locks in with a soft chime and a one line reason, for example: A bag of cement is much heavier than 1 kg, so kg.
tool_config.done_when: All five cards are done: the balance has been used for each of the seven things on Anu's list, each tag is in a bin, and the student has seen why 40 g, 30 g and 50 g cannot be the weight of an almirah, a sofa and a refrigerator.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): put the pencil on the left pan against the 1 kg block. Which side goes down? Answer: the 1 kg block side goes down, because a pencil is lighter than 1 kg.

Card 2 (practice values): put the school bag, then the brick, on the left pan. Which side goes down each time? Answer: the thing's side goes down both times, because a school bag and a brick are heavier than 1 kg.

Card 3 (practice values): pick the tag that fits. The pencil is 6 g or 6 kg. The school bag is 4 g or 4 kg. Answer: the pencil is 6 g, because 6 kg is 6,000 g, far too heavy for a pencil; the school bag is 4 kg, because 4 g is lighter than a pencil.

Card 4 (practice values): sort the three cards into the grams bin and the kilograms bin: an egg 50 g, a bag of cement 50 kg, a sugar sachet 5 g. Answer: the egg and the sugar sachet go in the grams bin, because they are lighter than 1 kg; the bag of cement goes in the kilograms bin, because it is much heavier than 1 kg.

Challenge: 'Anu has recorded the weights of the items in her house. Check if she has recorded them correctly by putting a tick against them if they look correct. 1. Iron Almirah: 40 g; 2. Bed: 60 kg; 3. Rice Bag: 5 kg; 4. Sofa: 30 g; 5. Bucket: 1 kg 800 g; 6. Water Bottle: 650 g; 7. Refrigerator: 50 g.' Put each thing on the balance, read its tag against 1 kg = 1,000 g and drop the tag in a bin. Sample answer: Bed, Rice Bag, Bucket and Water Bottle look right; Iron Almirah, Sofa and Refrigerator do not, because 40 g, 30 g and 50 g are far less than 1,000 g. The bed, the bucket and the bottle are matters of judgement, so your answer may differ.

hint_ladder.text: What does the right pan hold? How heavy is it in grams? Look at which side of the balance goes down.
Is the thing heavier or lighter than the 1 kg block? A heavier thing must weigh 1 kg or more, which is 1,000 g or more.
Read the tag. Is it more or less than 1,000 g? Is g or kg the unit for a thing this heavy or this light?
The almirah is far heavier than 1 kg, but 40 g is less than 1,000 g. Drop the tag in Does not look right.

student_does: Look at Anu's room and her list from the story. Anu says an iron almirah weighs 40 g. Put the iron almirah on the balance against the 1 kg block and watch which side goes down, then press Next.

Put a pencil, a school bag and a brick on the balance (practice values), pick the unit tag that fits each one, sort three more practice cards into the grams bin and the kilograms bin, and tell which weights are heavier or lighter than 1 kg.
Answer the book's question on Anu's list. Put each of the seven things against the 1 kg block, read its tag and drop the tag in Looks right or Does not look right.

4. 4 kg in grams is 4 × 1,000 = 4,000 g.

Answer: The pencil is 6 g, the school bag is 4 kg, and 4 kg is 4,000 g

content.text:
1. $1\text{ kg}$ is $1,000\text{ g}$. Use the $1\text{ kg}$ block as a guide: a thing that is heavier than the block must weigh $1\text{ kg}$ or more.
2. Iron Almirah: $40\text{ g}$. An almirah is far heavier than $1\text{ kg}$, but $40\text{ g}$ is much less than $1,000\text{ g}$. This does not look right.
3. Bed: $60\text{ kg}$. A bed is heavy, and $60\text{ kg}$ is much more than $1\text{ kg}$. This looks right.
[Image: Check! Check!: Ans1: solution]
4. Rice Bag: $5\text{ kg}$. A rice bag is heavier than $1\text{ kg}$, and $5\text{ kg}$ looks right.
5. Sofa: $30\text{ g}$. A sofa is far heavier than $1\text{ kg}$, but $30\text{ g}$ is much less than $1,000\text{ g}$. This does not look right.
6. Bucket: $1\text{ kg}\; 800\text{ g}$. This is more than $1\text{ kg}$, and a bucket can weigh this much. It looks right.
7. Water Bottle: $650\text{ g}$. This is less than $1\text{ kg}$, and a bottle of water can weigh this much. It looks right.
8. Refrigerator: $50\text{ g}$. A refrigerator is far heavier than $1\text{ kg}$, but $50\text{ g}$ is much less than $1,000\text{ g}$. This does not look right.
9. Check: the three weights $40\text{ g}$, $30\text{ g}$ and $50\text{ g}$ are all far less than $1,000\text{ g}$, which is $1\text{ kg}$.
Answer: Sample answer: ticks on Bed, Rice Bag, Bucket and Water Bottle; crosses on Iron Almirah, Sofa and Refrigerator. Your answer may differ for the bed, the bucket and the bottle.

media.title: Scale Reader
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Scale Reader

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M1.S4.T4.C9.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Weight and Capacity, "Let Us Do": "Read the scales", six round scales (a) to (f), full turns 4 kg, 2 kg, 6 kg, 4 kg, 1 kg, 1 kg, needle on the 6th, 18th, 25th, 26th, 15th and 66th mark counted clockwise from 0 (developer only). Needle positions in Activities 1 to 5 are practice values.

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student reads a needle on a round weighing scale by finding what one small mark stands for and then counting the marks from 0 to the needle.
- Out of scope: adding or comparing weights, digital scales, scales whose 0 is not at the top, the kg and g conversion rules beyond writing the reading.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- A round dial scale stands on a wooden market counter, about 75% of the stage height. Its face has a red 0 at the top, the labels 1 kg, 2 kg, 3 kg, 4 kg, and 40 small marks. The needle rests on the red 0.
- Instruction line: "Tap 0, then tap the 1 kg label."
- The child is invited to tap the red 0.

2. Scene and Objects
- Background: a wooden market counter in soft daylight with a cloth bag hanging blurred behind (photo).
- The dial (code-drawn): cream face, black marks, steel rim, black needle with a round hub. The red 0 is the only red number. A tall mark sits at every label and a short mark between. The needle snaps to marks only.
- The four faces (0 at the top, marks counted clockwise from 0):
  - 4 kg face: labels 1 kg (3 o'clock), 2 kg (6), 3 kg (9), 4 kg (top, beside the 0); 40 marks; one mark is 100 g.
  - 2 kg face: labels 1 kg (bottom) and 2 kg (top); 20 marks; one mark is 100 g.
  - 6 kg face: labels 1 kg to 6 kg, every sixth of a turn; 60 marks; one mark is 100 g.
  - 1 kg face: labels 250 g (3 o'clock), 500 g (6), 750 g (9), 1 kg (top); 100 marks; one mark is 10 g.
- Under the dial a wooden base holds the answer boxes, "kg" and "g" (or only "g"), each about 12% of the stage width. A round "Count marks" button sits on the stand; a bubble at the hub shows "n marks after 0". Three chips "1 g", "10 g", "100 g" appear above the dial when a card asks. Goal chip at the top left; in the star challenge six round tabs "a" to "f" sit along the top.

3. Main Interaction
- Tap a label: it rings. Tap two labels that are next to each other (0 counts): the arc between them lights, and two read-outs appear: the weight between them (for example "1 kg is 1,000 g") and the number of gaps ("10 gaps").
- Drag the needle round the dial: it snaps to the nearest mark and the bubble shows the marks after 0.
- Tap "Count marks": the marks light one at a time from 0 to the needle with a soft tick, and the bubble counts up.
- Tap an answer box: a large number pad opens. Boxes accept up to 5 digits.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset", and one main button "Check" that turns into "Next" when the step is right. Reset returns the needle and the boxes of this card to the start. Retry is always free.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Tap 0, then tap the 1 kg label." Goal chip: "One mark = ?" Setup: the 4 kg face, needle on 0. The child taps 0 and the 1 kg label; the arc lights and shows "1 kg is 1,000 g" and "10 gaps". Guess: before any dividing, the child taps one of the chips "1 g", "10 g", "100 g". Result: the right chip turns green with a bounce, the 10 gaps light one by one, and the strip says "1,000 ÷ 10 = 100 g. One mark stands for 100 g." Help: guided, arc and gap count shown.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Move the needle to 300 g." Goal chip: "300 g". Setup: the 4 kg face, the chip "1 mark = 100 g" stays on screen. Guess: before dragging, the child taps how many marks: "3", "30" or "300". The child then drags the needle. Result: the needle lands on the 3rd mark and the strip says "300 ÷ 100 = 3, so the needle goes 3 marks after 0." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Move the needle to 1 kg 200 g." Goal chip: "1 kg 200 g". Setup: the 4 kg face, no chip. Guess: before dragging, the child taps "Before the 1 kg label" or "Past the 1 kg label". The child finds one mark by tapping labels, then drags the needle. Result: the needle lands on the 12th mark, which is 2 marks past the 1 kg label, and the strip says "1,200 ÷ 100 = 12 marks: 10 marks to the 1 kg label and 2 marks more." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Read the needle. Write the weight." Goal chip: "Read the weight". Setup: the 2 kg face; the tool puts the needle on the 14th mark and it cannot be moved. Guess: before counting, the child taps "Less than 1 kg" or "More than 1 kg". The child taps 0 and the 1 kg label to find one mark, taps "Count marks", then types kg and g. Result: strip "14 × 100 = 1,400 g, which is 1 kg 400 g." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (independent). Goal line: "The needle is on the 8th mark on both scales. Read both." Goal chip: "Same spot, two scales". Setup: the 4 kg face and the 1 kg face, one after the other, each with the needle on the 8th mark after 0. Guess: before reading, the child taps "Same weight" or "Different weights". The child finds one mark on each face and types each reading in the g box. Result: the strip says "8 × 100 = 800 g on the first scale. 8 × 10 = 80 g on the second scale. The marks stand for different weights." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent). Goal line, in the book's words: "Read the scales. Write the correct weight in the space given below." Goal chip: "Read all 6 scales". Setup: tabs a to f, one scale at a time. (a) 4 kg face, needle on the 6th mark; (b) 2 kg face, 18th mark; (c) 6 kg face, 25th mark; (d) 4 kg face, 26th mark; (e) 1 kg face, 15th mark; (f) 1 kg face, 66th mark. Answer boxes as in the book: (a), (e), (f) one g box; (b), (c), (d) a kg box and a g box. Guess: the child commits by typing, then presses Check. Result lines: (a) "6 × 100 = 600 g." (b) "18 × 100 = 1,800 g, which is 1 kg 800 g." (c) "25 × 100 = 2,500 g, which is 2 kg 500 g." (d) "26 × 100 = 2,600 g, which is 2 kg 600 g." (e) "15 × 10 = 150 g." (f) "66 × 10 = 660 g." Each tab gets a tick. Help: independent; Count marks and the label taps stay available.

5. Mathematical Understanding
- The small marks do not always stand for 1 g: one mark is the weight between two labels divided by the number of gaps. The reading is the marks counted from 0 times the weight of one mark; the same needle spot reads differently on different scales.
- Rules in the child's words: "Start at 0 and go round like a clock." "First find what one mark stands for, then count."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the boxes turn green, the needle bounces gently, the strip shows the working with the real numbers, the pill gets a tick.
- Writes the nearest label, for example 1 kg when the needle is past it -> "The needle is past the 1 kg label, so the weight is more than 1 kg. Count the small marks after the label." The label and the marks after it pulse.
- Treats every mark as 1 g, for example writes 14 g -> "Here one mark stands for 100 g, not 1 g. 14 marks make 14 × 100 g." The arc between two labels lights.
- Puts the g number in the kg box -> "1,400 g is 1 kg 400 g. Put the whole kilograms in the kg box." Both boxes pulse.
- Writes the marks as grams after the kg, for example 1 kg 4 g -> "4 marks are 4 × 100 = 400 g, not 4 g."
- Off by one, counts the red 0 as a mark -> "The red 0 is not a mark. The first mark after it is mark 1." The first mark pulses.
- Activity 1, taps "1 g" -> "1,000 g is shared by 10 gaps. Each gap is more than 1 g." Taps "10 g" -> "10 gaps of 10 g make only 100 g. The labels are 1,000 g apart."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Where does the needle start? Follow the face from the red 0 and tap two labels next to each other." (2) visual clue: the arc between two neighbouring labels lights with the weight between them and the gaps. (3) almost the answer: the marks light one by one up to the needle and the bubble shows how many; the child still multiplies.
- Edge cases: on the 4 kg face the 4 kg label and the red 0 sit at the same spot; a needle there reads 0 g: "The needle is on 0, so nothing is weighed: 0 g." A needle exactly on a label reads that label with no marks after it. Scales (a) and (d), and (e) and (f), share a face with a different needle.

7. Ending
- Star Challenge 1 is done when all six tabs have a tick.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Start at 0 and go round like a clock." "One mark stands for the weight between two labels divided by the number of gaps." "Count the marks, then multiply by what one mark stands for." Think and talk: "Why can the needle on the same mark read 800 g on one scale and 80 g on another?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: a wooden market counter photo with a blurred hanging cloth bag; a stainless steel scale stand and base cut-out (photo-style); the round dials are code-drawn from the numbers above (face, marks, labels, needle, hub); a round "Count marks" button; a small wooden answer panel; number pad. Simple English, short lines.

Worked example: A scale has 0 at the top and the labels 1 kg to 5 kg round the face, so one full turn is 5 kg. Between two labels there are 5 equal gaps. The needle is on the 3rd mark after the 3 kg label. What is the weight? These are practice values.
1. Between two labels there is 1 kg, which is 1,000 g, shared into 5 equal gaps. 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 g, so one mark is 200 g.
2. The last label the needle has passed is 3 kg. 3 kg is 3,000 g.
3. The needle is 3 marks after 3 kg. 3 × 200 = 600 g.
4. Add: 3,000 g + 600 g = 3,600 g, which is 3 kg 600 g.
5. Check: 3 kg 600 g is between the 3 kg label and the 4 kg label, and the needle is between them.
Answer: The weight is 3 kg 600 g

1. Predict first: the needle is on the 6th mark after 0 on two different scales. On one scale the weight is 600 g. Can it be 60 g on the other?
2. Yes. Different scales have different small marks. One small mark does not always stand for 1 g.
3. To find what one mark stands for, take two labels that are next to each other. Find the weight between them and count the gaps between them.
4. The weight between two labels, divided by the number of gaps, is the weight of one mark.
5. Then read the needle: the last label it has passed, plus the marks counted times the weight of one mark.
6. Rule: first find what one mark stands for, then count.

content.text:
Worked example: A scale has a full turn of 2 kg. Its labels are 0, 500 g, 1 kg and 1 kg 500 g, and between two labels there are 10 equal gaps. The needle is on the 7th mark after the 1 kg 500 g label. What does one mark stand for, and what is the weight? These are practice values.
1. The weight between two labels is 500 g, and there are 10 gaps.
2. 500 ÷ 10 = 50 g, so one mark stands for 50 g.
3. The last label the needle has passed is 1 kg 500 g, which is 1,500 g.
4. The needle is 7 marks after that label. 7 × 50 = 350 g.
5. 1,500 g + 350 g = 1,850 g, which is 1 kg 850 g.
6. Check: 1 kg 850 g is more than 1 kg 500 g and less than 2 kg, which is the full turn.
Answer: One mark stands for 50 g and the weight is 1 kg 850 g

media.title: Kilogram and Gram Line
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Kilogram and Gram Line

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S6.T6.C14.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Weight and Capacity, "Different Units but Same Measure" (match the bags, the double number line), Shrenu's flour (3 kg 500 g, 2 kg 250 g), Shamim and Rehan's sugar (5 kg 50 g) and the six conversions with their line. Activities 1 to 4 use practice values (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student changes kilograms to grams and grams to kilograms on a double number line, and writes the grams part of a mixed weight in three places.
- Out of scope: milligrams, quintals, tonnes, adding or comparing weights.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- A wooden bakery counter (photo) with two flat kitchen scales with green displays side by side, the same checked cloth bag on each. The left display reads "11 kg"; the right display waits with "___ g".
- Along the counter's front board runs a double number line, about 90% of the stage width: top line kg, bottom line g. The left tick shows "1 kg" above and "1,000 g" below with a curved arrow "× 1,000" between; three more ticks are empty.
- Instruction line: "The same bag shows two numbers. Fill the g line." The child is invited to tap the arrow.

2. Scene and Objects
- Background: bakery counter, flour sack and bowl blurred. The bag: a checked cloth shopping bag with green tops (cut-out, about 12% of the stage width, on both scales). Scales: flat steel base, green display about 14% of the stage width, labelled "kg" and "g".
- The line: a teal tab "kg" and an amber tab "g" at the left; every tick has a slot above and below (an empty slot is a dashed box about 8% of the stage width). Wooden tiles (6 to 10, about 7% of the stage width each) sit on a shelf along the bottom.
- Arrow chips over and under the line carry labels "× 1,000", "÷ 1,000" or "× ___". A mixed weight card such as "13 kg 70 g" splits into a kg tile and a g tile, with a strip of three small squares (the "three places" strip) under the g tile. Goal chip at the top left.

3. Main Interaction
- Drag a tile onto a slot (one tile per slot): a right tile snaps in, a wrong one slides back with a short line. Tap an arrow chip to choose its label (the guess).
- Tap a mixed weight card to split it. Drag the kg tile under "× 1,000": it turns into thousands. Drop the g tile in the strip: it fills from the right and grey 0s fill the rest, so 70 shows as 070.
- Answer boxes (kg, and a three square g box that pads with grey zeros) take typed numbers from a large pad. In matching, drag from a kg card to a g card: a string draws, or springs back.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset", and one main button "Check" that turns into "Next". Retry is always free.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "The same bag shows two numbers. Fill the g line." Goal chip: "kg to g". Setup: top ticks 1 kg, 11 kg, 13 kg, 14 kg; bottom 1,000 g given and three empty slots; tiles 11,000 g, 13,000 g, 14,000 g, 1,100 g, 1,300 g. Guess: the child taps the arrow label: "× 10", "× 100" or "× 1,000", then drags the tiles. Result: strip "11 × 1,000 = 11,000 g. Every kg is 1,000 g." Help: guided, the first tick glows.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Now go back. Fill the kg line." Goal chip: "g to kg". Setup: bottom 1,000 g, 17,000 g, 22,000 g; top 1 kg and two empty slots; tiles 17 kg, 22 kg, 170 kg, 2,200 kg. Guess: the arrow label "× 1,000", "÷ 100" or "÷ 1,000". Result: "17,000 ÷ 1,000 = 17 kg. Going back, the number is 1,000 times smaller." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "Write 13 kg 70 g in grams." Goal chip: "kg and g to g". Setup: the card "13 kg 70 g". Guess: "1,370 g", "13,070 g" or "13,700 g". The child splits the card, drags 13 kg under "× 1,000" and drops 70 g in the three places strip. Result: "13 × 1,000 = 13,000 and 13,000 + 70 = 13,070 g. The 70 g takes three places: 070." Help: guided, grey zeros show.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Write 18,090 g in kg and g." Goal chip: "g to kg and g". Setup: the card "18,090 g". Guess: "18 kg 9 g", "18 kg 90 g" or "18 kg 900 g". The child types the kg box and the g box. Result: "18,090 − 18,000 = 90, so it is 18 kg 90 g. The g part is 090." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent), the book's words: "Bags are weighed on two different weighing balances. One weighing balance displays weight in kilograms and other displays weight in grams. Match the bags that have the same weights. You can use the double number line given below." Goal chip: "Match 6 bags". Part 1: kg cards 5 kg, 10 kg, 3 kg, 6 kg, 25 kg, 30 kg; g cards 3,000 g, 6,000 g, 10,000 g, 30,000 g, 5,000 g, 25,000 g; the child draws six strings (the strings are the guess). Each right pair shows "5 × 1,000 = 5,000 g" and so on, ending "Every g number is 1,000 times the kg number it matches." Part 2: the book's line, ticks as kg / g: 1 / 1,000; 3 / ___; 8 / ___; ___ / 15,000; 20 / ___; ___ / 25,000; 30 / ___, with "× 3" above and "× ___" below the first gap. Fills: 3, 3,000 g, 8,000 g, 15 kg, 20,000 g, 25 kg, 30,000 g. Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2 (independent), two cards in the book's words. Card A: "Shrenu is baking cakes for her shop. She needs 3 kg 500 g flour. Her kitchen scale measures only in grams. What should her kitchen scale show for 3 kg 500 g of flour?" Card B: "What would be 2 kg 250 g flour in grams?" Goal chip: "Show it in g". The child splits the card, uses "× 1,000" and the strip, and types the amount on the g only display. Results: "3 × 1,000 = 3,000 and 3,000 + 500 = 3,500 g." and "2 × 1,000 = 2,000 and 2,000 + 250 = 2,250 g."
- Star Challenge 3 (independent), the book's words: "Shamim and Rehan observed someone buying sugar weighing 5 kg 50 g. They thought of the quantity in grams. How much is it? One child says 5,050 g. The other says: No, it is 5,500 g. Who do you think is right and why?" Goal chip: "Who is right?" Two speech bubbles can be tapped (the children are never named). The child taps one, then proves it by splitting 5 kg 50 g. Result: "5 × 1,000 = 5,000 and 5,000 + 50 = 5,050 g. So 5,050 g is right. 5,500 g is 5 kg 500 g, a different weight."
- Star Challenge 4 (independent), the book's words: "Complete the conversions by filling in the blanks. You can use the double number line given below on which some numbers have been marked." Goal chip: "Six conversions". Tabs a to f: (a) 7 kg 67 g = ___ g; (b) 3 kg 300 g = ___ g; (c) 8 kg 69 g = ___ g; (d) 10,760 g = ___ kg ___ g; (e) 4,080 g = ___ kg ___ g; (f) 12,042 g = ___ kg ___ g. The helper line, ticks as kg / g: 1 / 1,000; 3 / ___; ___ / 4,000; 7 / ___; 8 / ___; ___ / 10,000; ___ / 12,000, then two dimmed end marks that refuse tiles. Fills: 3,000 g, 4 kg, 7,000 g, 8,000 g, 10 kg, 12 kg. Results: (a) 7,067 g, (b) 3,300 g, (c) 8,069 g, (d) 10 kg 760 g, (e) 4 kg 80 g, (f) 12 kg 42 g, each with a working line such as "7 × 1,000 = 7,000 and 7,000 + 67 = 7,067 g."

5. Mathematical Understanding
- The same weight is written in two units: every kg tick sits above a g tick with a number 1,000 times as big. In a mixed weight the kg part changes first and the g part takes three places (40 g is 040). Going back, the whole thousands are taken out.
- Rules in the child's words: "kg to g: × 1,000." "g to kg: ÷ 1,000." "The g part takes three places."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the tile snaps in with a gentle bounce, the tick turns green, the working shows.
- Picks "× 100", or a tile like 1,100 g for 11 kg, or 1,370 g for 13 kg 70 g -> "1 kg is 1,000 g, not 100 g. Use × 1,000." The arrow label pulses.
- Goes back with a bigger number, for example 170 kg for 17,000 g -> "Going from g to kg the number gets smaller: ÷ 1,000."
- Puts the g part in the wrong place, for example 13,700 g for 13 kg 70 g -> "13,700 g is 13 kg 700 g. 70 g takes three places: 070." The strip pulses.
- Writes 18 kg 9 g for 18,090 g -> "090 is 90 g. Keep three places: 18,090 − 18,000 = 90."
- Taps the child who says 5,500 g -> "5,500 g is 5 kg 500 g. Split 5 kg 50 g again: the g part is 050."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "How many g make 1 kg? Look at the first tick." (2) visual clue: the "× 1,000" arrow and the first tick glow; the three places strip lights. (3) almost the answer: the tool does the kg part, for example "13 × 1,000 = 13,000", and leaves the g part.
- Edge cases: a g part of 0 (for example 5,000 g is 5 kg 0 g) shows 000 and "No g left over." A kg tile dropped on the g line slides back with "Kg tiles go on the top line and g tiles on the bottom line."

7. Ending
- Each star challenge is done when every part has a tick.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "kg to g: × 1,000. g to kg: ÷ 1,000." "The g part of a weight takes three places: 40 g is 040." Think and talk: "A bag weighs 3 kg 5 g. Is that 3,005 g or 3,500 g? How do you know?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: a bakery counter photo with a flour sack and bowl; two flat kitchen scales with green displays; a checked cloth shopping bag; wooden number tiles; two speech bubbles (children never named); Shrenu as a small flat drawing. Code-drawn: lines, arrows, the three places strip, strings. Simple English.

3. 16 kg in grams: 16 × 1,000 = 16,000 g.
4. 9,000 g in kilograms: 9,000 ÷ 1,000 = 9 kg.
5. Check: 9 × 1,000 = 9,000, so the number on each line matches the number on the other line.
Answer: 4 kg is 4,000 g, 16 kg is 16,000 g and 9,000 g is 9 kg

content.text:
1. Predict first: a weight is 6 kg 40 g. Is it 6,040 g or 6,400 g?
2. Change the kg part first: 6 kg is 6 × 1,000 = 6,000 g. Then add the g part: 6,000 + 40 = 6,040 g.
3. The g part takes three places because 1 kg is 1,000 g. 40 g is 040, so it goes next to the 6 as 6,040. 6,400 g would mean 6 kg 400 g.
4. To go back, take out the whole thousands. 11,205 g has 11 thousands, so it is 11 kg, and 205 g are left over. 11,205 g is 11 kg 205 g.
5. Rule: kg to g, multiply by 1,000 and add the g part in three places; g to kg and g, take out the thousands.

1. 6 kg 40 g: change the 6 kg first. 6 × 1,000 = 6,000 g.

3. A slip to avoid: 6,400 g is 6 kg 400 g, which is a different weight.
4. 11,205 g: take out the whole thousands. 11,205 − 11,000 = 205, so 11 thousands and 205 g are left over.
5. 11 thousands of grams are 11 kg, so 11,205 g is 11 kg 205 g.
6. Check: 11 × 1,000 = 11,000 and 11,000 + 205 = 11,205.
Answer: 6 kg 40 g is 6,040 g and 11,205 g is 11 kg 205 g

content.text:
1. $5\text{ kg}\; 50\text{ g}$: change the $5\text{ kg}$ first. $5 \times 1,000 = 5,000\text{ g}$.
2. Add the gram part. $50\text{ g}$ takes three places, $050$. $5,000 + 50 = 5,050\text{ g}$.
3. So $5\text{ kg}\; 50\text{ g}$ is $5,050\text{ g}$, and the child who says $5,050\text{ g}$ is right.
4. The other child says $5,500\text{ g}$. But $5,500\text{ g}$ is $5,000\text{ g} + 500\text{ g}$, which is $5\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$, a different weight.
5. Check: $5,050 - 5,000 = 50$, so $50\text{ g}$ are left over after $5\text{ kg}$.
Answer: $5,050\text{ g}$ is right: $5\text{ kg}\; 50\text{ g}$ is $5,000\text{ g} + 50\text{ g}$. $5,500\text{ g}$ would be $5\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: which is heavier, 4 kg 200 g or 4,020 g? You cannot compare the numbers 4,200 and 4,020 until both weights are in the same unit. Change both to grams. 4 kg 200 g is 4,200 g. The other weight is already 4,020 g. 4,200 is more than 4,020, so 4 kg 200 g is heavier. If a weight is a sum, work out the sum first. 1 kg 250 g + 750 g is 1,250 + 750 = 2,000 g, which is 2 kg. To put weights in order, change all of them to grams and order the numbers. Rule: change to the same unit first, then compare the numbers. 1. Change both weights to grams. 4 kg 200 g is 4 × 1,000 + 200 = 4,200 g. 2. The other weight is 4,020 g. Compare the numbers: 4,200 is more than 4,020. 3. So 4 kg 200 g > 4,020 g. 4. Work out the sum first. 1 kg 250 g is 1,250 g, and 1,250 + 750 = 2,000 g. 5. 2 kg is 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 g. 6. 2,000 g and 2,000 g are the same, so 1 kg 250 g + 750 g = 2 kg. 7. Check: 4,200 − 4,020 = 180, so the first weight is 180 g more. Answer: 4 kg 200 g > 4,020 g, and 1 kg 250 g + 750 g = 2 kg

1. Predict first: a big load is 6 times as heavy as a load of 3,000 kg. Do you multiply or divide to find the big load?
2. 6 times as heavy means 6 loads of the same weight. Multiply: 3,000 × 6 = 18,000 kg.
3. To go back, divide. If a load is 9 times as heavy as a small load, divide its weight by 9 to find the small load.
4. Rule: n times as heavy, multiply to go up and divide to come back.

content.text:
Worked example: A load is 6 times as heavy as a load of 3,000 kg. How heavy is it? Another load weighs 450 kg and is 9 times as heavy as a small load. How heavy is the small load? These are practice values.
1. 6 times as heavy means 6 copies of 3,000 kg. Multiply: 3,000 × 6 = 18,000 kg.
2. The second load is 9 times as heavy as the small load, so 9 copies of the small load make 450 kg.
3. Divide to find one copy: 450 ÷ 9 = 50 kg.
4. Check: 50 × 9 = 450, the weight of the second load.
Answer: The first load is 18,000 kg and the small load is 50 kg

media.teaching_notes: 1. Change both weights to the same unit and compare. 2. (a): 20 g is 20 × 1,000 = 20,000 mg. 20,000 is more than 200, so 20 g > 200 mg. 3. (b): 16 g 50 mg is 16,000 + 50 = 16,050 mg. 50 g 16 mg is 50,000 + 16 = 50,016 mg. 16,050 is less than 50,016, so 16 g 50 mg < 50 g 16 mg. 4. (c): 2 g 100 mg is 2,000 + 100 = 2,100 mg. 2,010 is less than 2,100, so 2,010 mg < 2 g 100 mg. 5. (d): 9,000 mg is 9,000 ÷ 1,000 = 9 g. 9 g is less than 90 g, so 9,000 mg < 90 g. 6. (e): both are in g. 5,000 is less than 7,500, so 5,000 g < 7,500 g. 7. (f): 800 mg + 88 mg is 888 mg and 880 mg + 8 mg is 888 mg. They are the same, so 800 mg + 88 mg = 880 mg + 8 mg. 8. Check: in every part both weights were in the same unit before they were compared. Answer: (a): >; (b): <; (c): <; (d): <; (e): <; (f): =

content.text:
1. Change both weights to the same unit and compare.
2. $(a)$: $20\text{ g}$ is $20 \times 1,000 = 20,000\text{ mg}$. $20,000$ is more than $200$, so $20\text{ g} > 200\text{ mg}$.
3. $(b)$: $16\text{ g}\; 50\text{ mg}$ is $16,000 + 50 = 16,050\text{ mg}$. $50\text{ g}\; 16\text{ mg}$ is $50,000 + 16 = 50,016\text{ mg}$. $16,050$ is less than $50,016$, so $16\text{ g}\; 50\text{ mg} < 50\text{ g}\; 16\text{ mg}$.
4. $(c)$: $2\text{ g}\; 100\text{ mg}$ is $2,000 + 100 = 2,100\text{ mg}$. $2,010$ is less than $2,100$, so $2,010\text{ mg} < 2\text{ g}\; 100\text{ mg}$.
5. $(d)$: $9,000\text{ mg}$ is $9,000 \div 1,000 = 9\text{ g}$. $9\text{ g}$ is less than $90\text{ g}$, so $9,000\text{ mg} < 90\text{ g}$.
6. $(e)$: both are in grams. $5,000$ is less than $7,500$, so $5,000\text{ g} < 7,500\text{ g}$.
[Image: Let Us Find: Ans4: solution]
7. $(f)$: $800\text{ mg} + 88\text{ mg}$ is $888\text{ mg}$ and $880\text{ mg} + 8\text{ mg}$ is $888\text{ mg}$. They are the same, so $800\text{ mg} + 88\text{ mg} = 880\text{ mg} + 8\text{ mg}$.
8. Check: in every part both weights were in the same unit before they were compared.
Answer: $(a)$: $>$; $(b)$: $<$; $(c)$: $<$; $(d)$: $<$; $(e)$: $<$; $(f)$: $=$
[Image: Let Us Find: Ans4: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. $100\text{ kg}$ is $1$ quintal and $10$ quintals is $1$ tonne.
2. $(a)$: $5,000 \div 100 = 50$, so $5,000\text{ kg}$ is $50$ quintals.
3. $50 \div 10 = 5$, so $50$ quintals is $5$ tonne.
4. $(b)$: $9,000 \div 100 = 90$, so $9,000\text{ kg}$ is $90$ quintals.
5. $(c)$: $1$ tonne is $1,000\text{ kg}$, so $8$ tonnes is $8 \times 1,000 = 8,000\text{ kg}$.
6. Check: $5 \times 1,000 = 5,000\text{ kg}$ and $90 \times 100 = 9,000\text{ kg}$.
Answer: $(a)$: $50$ quintals, $5$ tonne; $(b)$: $90$ quintals; $(c)$: $8,000\text{ kg}$

media.title: Weight Regrouper
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Weight Regrouper

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S16.T16.C53.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Weight and Capacity, "The Grocery Store": Examples 4 and 5 (Rathna's rice) and Let Us Do questions 1 to 7. Numbers of Activities 1 to 4 and the Practice are practice values (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student adds and subtracts weights in kg and g by exchanging 1,000 g for 1 kg when adding, and breaking 1 kg into 1,000 g when the g on top are fewer.
- Out of scope: multiplying or sharing weights, comparing weights.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- A grocery counter (photo) with rice and flour sacks behind. Two wooden trays stand on it, kg left and g right, about 28% of the stage width each, with a small crate between them marked "1,000 g make 1 kg". Above hangs a sum board (columns "kg" and "g", rows "4 kg 300 g" and "2 kg 400 g", a "+", an empty result row).
- On the counter lie 4 bags and 3 packets, then 2 bags and 4 packets. Instruction line: "Put each weight in its tray. Add them." The child is invited to drag a bag.

2. Scene and Objects
- Chips (photo cut-outs): a "1 kg" cloth bag (about 9% of the stage width) and a "100 g" paper packet (about 4%). Trays show live totals. The crate lights with the button "Exchange 1,000 g for 1 kg" at 1,000 g or more. Subtraction cards add a "Take away" box.
- The sum board has a carry cell above the kg column, a "+" or "−" chip and a result row with kg and g cells. In the Practice and the star challenges only the board and the question stay. Goal chip at the top left.

3. Main Interaction
- Drag chips into a tray or back out. Exchange: tap the crate button: ten packets bundle into a bag that flies to the kg tray. Break: tap "Break 1 kg into 1,000 g" when the g on top are too few: a bag opens into ten packets. Take away: drag chips to the box.
- On the board: tap "+" or "−", tap a result cell for a number pad, tap the lit button.
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset", and one main button "Check" that turns into "Next". Retry is always free.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Put each weight in its tray. Add them." Goal chip: "Add, no exchange". Setup: 4 kg 300 g + 2 kg 400 g. Guess: "Will the g tray reach 1,000 g?" with "Yes", "No". The child drags the chips into the trays. Result: "g: 300 + 400 = 700 g, less than 1,000 g, so no exchange. kg: 4 + 2 = 6. The weight is 6 kg 700 g." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Add them. Exchange when the g tray is full." Goal chip: "Add, exchange". Setup: 3 kg 800 g + 2 kg 600 g. Guess: the same. At the tenth packet the crate lights and the child taps exchange. Result: "g: 800 + 600 = 1,400 g. Exchange 1,000 g for 1 kg: 400 g are left. kg: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The weight is 6 kg 400 g." Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "Take the small weight away from the big one." Goal chip: "Subtract, no break". Setup: 7 kg 900 g − 2 kg 300 g. Guess: "Can you take 300 g from 900 g?" with "Yes", "No". The child drags 2 bags and 3 packets to the box. Result: "g: 900 − 300 = 600 g. kg: 7 − 2 = 5. 5 kg 600 g are left." Help: guided.
- Activity 4 (guided). Goal line: "Take away 1 kg 500 g. There are too few g." Goal chip: "Subtract, break 1 kg". Setup: 6 kg 200 g − 1 kg 500 g. Guess: "Can you take 500 g from 200 g?" with "Yes", "No". Dragging 5 packets fails (only 2 exist): the box shakes and the break button lights. After the break the child takes away 1 bag and 5 packets. Result: "6 kg 200 g becomes 5 kg 1,200 g. g: 1,200 − 500 = 700 g. kg: 5 − 1 = 4. 4 kg 700 g are left." Help: guided.
- Practice (independent), one sum on the board with no chips. Goal chip: "Your turn". Sum: 5 kg 700 g + 1 kg 800 g. Guess: "Will you exchange?" with "Yes", "No". Result: "700 + 800 = 1,500 g. Exchange: 500 g are left. 5 + 1 + 1 = 7 kg. 7 kg 500 g." Help: independent.
- Every star card is independent: the question sits above the board with its numbers in the two rows. Guess: the child taps "+" or "−", types the g cell, taps Exchange or Break when it lights, types the kg cell and presses Check. The working shown below is each result.
- Star Challenge 1. Card A, the book's words: "Rathna went to the local grocery store and bought several items. She bought 2 kg 500 g rice for daily use and 1 kg 750 g additional rice for the upcoming Pongal festival. How much total rice did she buy?" Working: 500 + 750 = 1,250 g, exchange, 250 g left; 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 kg. Answer: 4 kg 250 g. Card B: "How much extra rice did she buy for household use than for the Pongal festival?" Working: 500 g is fewer than 750 g, so break: 1 kg 1,500 g; 1,500 − 750 = 750 g; 1 − 1 = 0 kg. Answer: 750 g.
- Star Challenge 2. Card A: "A restaurant owner uses 5 kg 200 g, 8 kg 900 g, and 12 kg 600 g of onions over 3 days. What is the total weight of onions used by the restaurant owner in 3 days?" Working: 200 + 900 + 600 = 1,700 g, exchange, 700 g left; 5 + 8 + 12 + 1 = 26 kg. Answer: 26 kg 700 g. Card B: "Aarav is helping his grandfather at the fruit stall. He lifts two baskets of apples weighing 2 kg 100 g and 3 kg 950 g. What is the total weight of apples he lifted?" Working: 100 + 950 = 1,050 g, exchange, 50 g left; 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 kg. Answer: 6 kg 50 g.
- Star Challenge 3. Card A: "4 kg 500 g of sand is used from a sack weighing 10 kg. How much sand is left in the sack?" Working: 10 kg has no g, so break: 9 kg 1,000 g; 1,000 − 500 = 500 g; 9 − 4 = 5 kg. Answer: 5 kg 500 g. Card B: "A rice sack weighs 9 kg 750 g. After some rice is used, it weighs 3 kg 700 g. How much rice was used?" Working: 750 − 700 = 50 g, no break; 9 − 3 = 6 kg. Answer: 6 kg 50 g.
- Star Challenge 4. Card A: "A delivery truck delivered 17 kg 900 g of supplies in the morning and 12 kg 700 g in the afternoon. How much total supplies did it deliver?" Working: 900 + 700 = 1,600 g, exchange, 600 g left; 17 + 12 + 1 = 30 kg. Answer: 30 kg 600 g. Card B: "A box of books weighs 14 kg 750 g. After removing some books, the weight of the box is 10 kg 500 g. What is the weight of the books removed?" Working: 750 − 500 = 250 g; 14 − 10 = 4 kg. Answer: 4 kg 250 g.
- Star Challenge 5 (one question, two steps): "In a community kitchen of a Gurdwara, 65 kg of flour was purchased on one day. Out of this, 42 kg 275 g flour was used for preparing langar. The next day, an additional 52 kg 500 g of flour was bought. What is the total quantity of flour now available in the kitchen store?" Step 1, "−": break 1 kg: 64 kg 1,000 g; 1,000 − 275 = 725 g; 64 − 42 = 22 kg; 22 kg 725 g are left. That result moves up as the first row of step 2, "+ 52 kg 500 g": 725 + 500 = 1,225 g, exchange, 225 g left; 22 + 52 + 1 = 75 kg. Answer: 75 kg 225 g.

5. Mathematical Understanding
- Weights add like with like, and 1,000 g is exactly 1 kg: ten 100 g packets bundle into one bag. A full g column is exchanged for 1 kg; a short g column on top is topped up by a break.
- Rules in the child's words: "Add kg with kg and g with g." "1,000 g or more? Exchange for 1 kg." "Too few g on top? Break 1 kg into 1,000 g."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: result cells turn green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick.
- Leaves 1,250 g in the g cell -> "1,000 g or more is 1 kg. Exchange first." The exchange button glows.
- Forgets the exchanged 1 kg -> "Do not forget the 1 kg from the exchange." The carry cell pulses.
- Takes the smaller g from the bigger, for example 800 − 200 -> "You cannot take 800 g from 200 g. Break 1 kg into 1,000 g first." The break button glows.
- Taps "+" for "left", "used" or "removed" -> "Some was taken away, so use −." Taps "−" for "total" -> "The weights are put together, so use +."
- Breaks when no break is needed -> "No break is needed: 750 g is more than 700 g."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Which column do you start with, kg or g? Is the g column 1,000 g or more?" (2) visual clue: the g column glows and the exchange or break button pulses. (3) almost the answer: the tool does the exchange or break and shows the new columns; the child finishes.
- Edge cases: a g column of exactly 1,000 g leaves 0 g, and an empty cell gets "An empty place is not a zero: write 0 g." A result of 0 kg, as in the extra rice, needs "0" typed; the strip says "0 kg 750 g is 750 g."

7. Ending
- Each star challenge is done when its cards are checked.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Add kg with kg and g with g." "1,000 g is 1 kg: exchange to add, break to subtract." Think and talk: "Why can you not take 800 g from 200 g? What do you do?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: a grocery counter photo with rice and flour sacks; two wooden trays; a small wooden crate; a "1 kg" cloth bag and a "100 g" paper packet (front-facing cut-outs); a "Take away" cardboard box. Code-drawn: the board, columns, carry cell and the exchange animation. Simple English.

Way 1, in parts: add the kg, 3 + 2 = 5 kg. Add the g, 600 + 700 = 1,300 g. Since 1,000 g = 1 kg, 1,300 g is 1 kg 300 g. So the weight is 5 kg + 1 kg 300 g = 6 kg 300 g. Add the kilograms: 3 + 2 = 5 kg. 2. Add the grams: 600 + 700 = 1,300 g. 1,000 g is 1 kg, so 1,300 g is 1 kg 300 g. 3. Put the parts together: 5 kg + 1 kg 300 g = 6 kg 300 g. 4. Way 2, in a column. Way 3, in grams. 3 kg 600 g is 3,600 g and 2 kg 700 g is 2,700 g. 3,600 + 2,700 = 6,300 g. 7. 6,300 g is 6 kg 300 g. All three ways give the same weight. Answer: 3 kg 600 g + 2 kg 700 g = 6 kg 300 g

content.question: A restaurant owner uses 5 kg 200 g, 8 kg 900 g, and 12 kg 600 g of onions over 3 days. What is the total weight of onions used by the restaurant owner in 3 days?
content.book_number: Let Us Do: onions
content.question_tex: A restaurant owner uses $5\text{ kg}\; 200\text{ g}$, $8\text{ kg}\; 900\text{ g}$, and $12\text{ kg}\; 600\text{ g}$ of onions over $3$ days. What is the total weight of onions used by the restaurant owner in $3$ days?
content.publication_text: A restaurant owner uses $5\text{ kg}\; 200\text{ g}$, $8\text{ kg}\; 900\text{ g}$, and $12\text{ kg}\; 600\text{ g}$ of onions over $3$ days. What is the total weight of onions used by the restaurant owner in $3$ days?

content.text:
1. Add the three weights: $5\text{ kg}\; 200\text{ g} + 8\text{ kg}\; 900\text{ g} + 12\text{ kg}\; 600\text{ g}$.
2. Add the kilograms: $5 + 8 + 12 = 25\text{ kg}$.
3. Add the grams: $200 + 900 + 600 = 1,700\text{ g}$. $1,700\text{ g}$ is $1\text{ kg}\; 700\text{ g}$.
4. $25\text{ kg} + 1\text{ kg}\; 700\text{ g} = 26\text{ kg}\; 700\text{ g}$.
5. Check in grams: $5,200 + 8,900 + 12,600 = 26,700\text{ g}$, which is $26\text{ kg}\; 700\text{ g}$.
Answer: $26\text{ kg}\; 700\text{ g}$

content.text:
1. The flour left after the langar is $65\text{ kg} - 42\text{ kg}\; 275\text{ g}$. Then add the flour bought the next day, $52\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$.
2. Change to grams: $65\text{ kg}$ is $65,000\text{ g}$, $42\text{ kg}\; 275\text{ g}$ is $42,275\text{ g}$ and $52\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$ is $52,500\text{ g}$.
3. $65,000 - 42,275 = 22,725\text{ g}$.
4. $22,725 + 52,500 = 75,225\text{ g}$.
5. $75,225\text{ g}$ is $75\text{ kg}\; 225\text{ g}$.
6. Check: $75,225 - 52,500 = 22,725$ and $22,725 + 42,275 = 65,000$.
Answer: $75\text{ kg}\; 225\text{ g}$ of flour

content.text: A farmer weighs a sack of potatoes and finds it to be $10\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$. If the farmer has $4$ such potato sacks, what is the total weight of all the sacks?
content.question: A farmer weighs a sack of potatoes and finds it to be 10 kg 500 g. If the farmer has 4 such potato sacks, what is the total weight of all the sacks?
content.book_number: Example 6: the farmer's sacks
content.question_tex: A farmer weighs a sack of potatoes and finds it to be $10\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$. If the farmer has $4$ such potato sacks, what is the total weight of all the sacks?
content.publication_text: A farmer weighs a sack of potatoes and finds it to be $10\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$. If the farmer has $4$ such potato sacks, what is the total weight of all the sacks?

content.text:
1. $4$ sacks of the same weight make $4$ times that weight: $4 \times 10\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$.
2. Multiply the kilograms: $4 \times 10 = 40\text{ kg}$.
3. Multiply the grams: $4 \times 500 = 2,000\text{ g}$. $1,000\text{ g}$ is $1\text{ kg}$, so $2,000\text{ g}$ is $2\text{ kg}$.
4. Add the parts: $40\text{ kg} + 2\text{ kg} = 42\text{ kg}$.
5. Check in grams: $10\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$ is $10,500\text{ g}$ and $10,500 \times 4 = 42,000\text{ g}$, which is $42\text{ kg}$.
Answer: The $4$ sacks weigh $42\text{ kg}$ in all

content.text:
1. Sharing equally into $4$ boxes means dividing by $4$: $4\text{ kg}\; 800\text{ g}\; \div 4$.

5. The question asks for grams. $1\text{ kg}$ is $1,000\text{ g}$, so $1\text{ kg}\; 200\text{ g}$ is $1,200\text{ g}$.
6. Check in grams: $4\text{ kg}\; 800\text{ g}$ is $4,800\text{ g}$ and $4,800 \div 4 = 1,200\text{ g}$.
Answer: Each small box weighs $1,200\text{ g} (1\text{ kg}\; 200\text{ g})$

media.title: Scaling Line
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Scaling Line

B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M2.S21.T21.C81.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity
- Textbook source: Weight and Capacity, the cost and scaling "Let Us Do" questions 1 to 4 (the cost table, 4 people and 500 g rice, 5 kg of tomatoes at ₹73, Nitesh the scrap dealer). Activities 1 to 4 use practice values (developer only).

C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student finds the missing number on a double number line by doing the same thing to both lines, and uses it to find the cost of a weight from the cost of 1 kg.
- Out of scope: unit conversion drills, dividing by numbers that do not divide evenly, more than two lines.

D. TOOL DESCRIPTION

1. Opening Screen
- A grocery stall price board (photo) with a double number line painted across it, about 90% of the stage width. Top row "parathas": "3" and "12". Bottom row "flour (g)": "90 g" and a dashed empty box. A curved arrow above and one below, with empty labels. A paper price tag and a small flour pan hang below.
- Instruction line: "3 parathas need 90 g of flour. How much flour do 12 parathas need?" The child is invited to tap a guess chip: "99 g", "360 g" or "1,080 g".

2. Scene and Objects
- The line is code-drawn on the board: two rows with equal ticks and a name chip at the left of each row (for example "kg" and "₹"); empty ticks are dashed boxes about 9% of the stage width.
- Arrow arcs sit over the top row and under the bottom row with a round label such as "× 4"; a pale ghost arc appears below once the top arc is set. A "Try adding instead" button sits on the board edge (Activity 2 only). The price tag shows a given price such as "₹80 for 1 kg". Star Challenge 1 has six item chips along the top: "Rice", "Flour", "Sugar", "Chana dal", "Besan", "Jaggery". Goal chip at the top left.

3. Main Interaction
- Tap an arc: choose "×" or "÷" and a number (chips such as "× 3", "× 4", "× 9" in guided cards; a number pad in independent ones). When the top arc is set, the bottom arc shows the same label and the child taps it to lock it. A row can hold two arcs, for example "÷ 10" then "× 6".
- Tap an empty tick: a number pad opens. A divide arc works only if the number divides evenly; otherwise it springs back with "That does not divide evenly. Try another number."
- Bottom buttons: "Hint", "Reset", and one main button "Check" that turns into "Next". Retry is always free.

4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "3 parathas need 90 g of flour. How much flour do 12 parathas need?" Goal chip: "3 to 12". Setup: top 3 and 12, bottom 90 g and an empty tick. Guess: the child taps "99 g", "360 g" or "1,080 g", then sets the top arc from "× 3", "× 4", "× 9", locks it below and types the number. Result: 360 g turns green (a different guess is not marked wrong); strip "3 to 12 is × 4, because 3 × 4 = 12. So 90 × 4 = 360 g." Help: guided.
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Try adding the same number to both lines." Goal chip: "Plus or times?" Setup: the same line. Guess: "Will adding 9 to both lines keep them in step?" with "Yes", "No". The child taps "Try adding instead": the arcs show "+ 9" and the bottom shows 99 g. Result: "3 + 9 = 12, but 90 + 9 = 99 g. 12 parathas are 4 times as many as 3, so they need 4 times the flour: 90 × 4 = 360 g." The arcs change to "× 4". Help: guided.
- Activity 3 (guided). Goal line: "Lentils cost ₹80 for 1 kg. What do 5 kg 250 g cost?" Goal chip: "Cost of 5 kg 250 g". Setup: line 1 top 1 kg and 5 kg, line 2 top 1,000 g and 250 g, each with bottom ₹80 and an empty tick. Guess: "Will it cost more than ₹400 or less?" with "More", "Less". The child sets "× 5" and types 400, sets "÷ 4" (chips "÷ 2", "÷ 4", "÷ 10") and types 20, then the total. Result: "5 × 80 = ₹400 for 5 kg. 250 g is a quarter of 1,000 g, so it costs 80 ÷ 4 = ₹20. 400 + 20 = ₹420." Help: guided.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "8 kg of potatoes cost ₹96. What does 1 kg cost?" Goal chip: "Cost of 1 kg". Setup: top 8 kg and 1 kg, bottom ₹96 and an empty tick. Guess: "Will 1 kg cost more or less than ₹96?" with "More", "Less". The child sets both arcs and types. Result: "8 kg down to 1 kg is ÷ 8. 96 ÷ 8 = ₹12." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1 (independent), the book's words: "The cost of some grocery items is given in the following table. Find the total cost of each item." Goal chip: "Find 6 total costs". Items, weight and cost of 1 kg: Rice 12 kg 500 g, ₹60; Flour 7 kg 250 g, ₹40; Sugar 5 kg, ₹45; Chana dal 3 kg 600 g, ₹70; Besan 4 kg, ₹60; Jaggery 1 kg 400 g, ₹50. Each item has a line for the whole kg, a line for the part of a kg if any, and a typed total. Guess: "More" or "The same": will the total be more than the whole kg alone? Results: Rice 12 × 60 = ₹720, 500 g costs 60 ÷ 2 = ₹30, total ₹750. Flour 7 × 40 = ₹280, 250 g costs 40 ÷ 4 = ₹10, total ₹290. Sugar 5 × 45 = ₹225. Chana dal 3 × 70 = ₹210, 100 g costs 70 ÷ 10 = ₹7, 600 g costs 6 × 7 = ₹42, total ₹252. Besan 4 × 60 = ₹240. Jaggery 1 × 50 = ₹50, 100 g costs 50 ÷ 10 = ₹5, 400 g costs 4 × 5 = ₹20, total ₹70. The strip names the part: "500 g is half of 1,000 g", "250 g is a quarter of 1,000 g", "100 g is a tenth of 1,000 g".
- Star Challenge 2 (independent), the book's words: "4 people need 500 g rice for a meal. How much rice will be needed for 8 people if they eat similar quantity of rice?" Goal chip: "4 people to 8 people". Setup: top 4 and 8 with "× 2" given, bottom 500 g and an empty tick and arc. The child types the bottom arc number and the amount. Result: "4 to 8 is × 2, so 500 × 2 = 1,000 g, which is 1 kg."
- Star Challenge 3 (independent), the book's words: "5 kg of tomatoes cost ₹73. How much will 10 kg of tomatoes cost?" Goal chip: "5 kg to 10 kg". Setup: top 5 kg and 10 kg with "× 2" given, bottom ₹73 and an empty tick and arc. Result: "5 to 10 is × 2, so 73 × 2 = ₹146."
- Star Challenge 4 (independent), the book's words: "Nitesh is a scrap dealer. How much would he have paid for (a) 16 kg of old newspaper, if he paid ₹8 for every 1 kg of newspaper? (b) 20 kg iron, if he paid ₹200 for every 10 kg of iron? (c) 10 kg plastic, if he paid ₹30 for 5 kg of plastic? Make double number lines for answering (b) and (c)." Goal chip: "Parts a, b, c". The child builds each line, bottom with an empty tick: (a) top 1 kg and 16 kg, ₹8; (b) top 10 kg and 20 kg, ₹200; (c) top 5 kg and 10 kg, ₹30. Results: (a) "1 to 16 is × 16, so 8 × 16 = ₹128." (b) "10 to 20 is × 2, so 200 × 2 = ₹400." (c) "5 to 10 is × 2, so 30 × 2 = ₹60."

5. Mathematical Understanding
- A double number line keeps two quantities in step: whatever is done to the top number is done to the bottom number. Adding the same number to both lines breaks the step. The cost of a weight is the whole kg times the cost of 1 kg, plus the cost of the part: 500 g is half of 1,000 g, 250 g a quarter, 100 g a tenth.
- Rules in the child's words: "Find what the top line was multiplied by, then do the same below." "Times, not plus."

6. Feedback and Hints
- Correct: the tick turns green with a gentle bounce, both arcs glow together, the pill gets a tick.
- Adds, for example 504 g for 8 people -> "4 people to 8 people is × 2, not + 4. Whatever you do to the top line, do to the bottom line." The top arc pulses.
- Bottom arc differs from the top -> "Both lines get the same arrow. The top line is × 2."
- Charges a full price for a part, for example ₹60 for 500 g of rice -> "500 g is half of 1,000 g, so it costs half of ₹60: 60 ÷ 2."
- Gives ₹7 for 600 g of chana dal -> "₹7 is for 100 g. 600 g is 6 times 100 g: × 6."
- Forgets to add the part -> "The part of a kg costs money too. Add it to the cost of the whole kg."
- Goes down with ×, for example × 8 from 8 kg to 1 kg -> "From 8 kg down to 1 kg the number gets smaller: ÷ 8."
- Hint button, 3 levels: (1) words: "Look at the top line. What happened to the first number to get the second?" (2) visual clue: the top arc glows and a ghost arc with the same number hovers below. (3) almost the answer: "The arrow is × 2. Multiply the bottom number by 2."
- Edge cases: a divide arc that does not divide evenly springs back. Sugar and besan have no part of a kg, so only the whole kg line opens: "No g left over, so no part to add."

7. Ending
- Each star challenge is done when every item or part has a tick.
- End screen: "Well done!" Remember: "Whatever you do to the top line, do to the bottom line." "Multiply or divide both lines by the same number. Do not add." "A part of a kg costs that part of the price of 1 kg." Think and talk: "Why does adding the same number to both lines not keep them in step?" Button: "Start again".

8. Assets and Language
- Images: a grocery stall photo in a market lane; a painted wooden price board; a paper price tag on a string; a small flour pan; six small photo cut-outs for the item chips; Nitesh with his cart (flat drawing). Code-drawn: line, ticks, arcs, number pad. Simple English.

tool_config.idea: Scale two linked quantities by the same number on a double number line, and find a cost from the cost of 1 kg: whatever happens to the top line happens to the bottom line, and adding the same number to both lines does not keep them in step.
tool_config.title: Scaling Line
tool_config.screen: The price board of the grocery stall in Anu's neighbourhood market, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A double number line is painted across the board and is the largest thing on screen: two rows with equal ticks, a pair of numbers given at the left of each row and a blank at the right (for example people above and grams below, or kg above and rupees below). Under the board are a price tag and a weighing pan. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the multiplier arrow along the top row and choose the number (× 2, × 3, × 10) or the divide arrow (÷ 2 for 500 g of 1 kg, ÷ 10 for 100 g of 1 kg); the same arrow then appears on the bottom row; number keys to type the missing value; a Try adding instead button that adds the same number to both rows and shows that they no longer match; Check, Hint, Retry (clears this line), Reset (restores all lines), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the multiplier arrow on each row, the missing value as typed, and a card number out of 7.
feedback: When the multiplier arrow is set the same arrow appears on the bottom row and the tool says so, for example: Top line × 3, so the bottom line × 3.
A bottom value that was found by adding is answered with the check, for example: 3 plates to 9 plates is times 3, not plus 6. Try × 3 on the bottom line too.
A cost that treats 500 g like 1 kg gets a clue, for example: 500 g is half of 1,000 g, so it costs half of ₹36.
A correct line shows the working in one line, for example: 5 kg to 10 kg is × 2, so ₹73 × 2 = ₹146.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): 3 plates need 240 g of lentils. How many grams do 9 plates need? Answer: the top line is × 3 because 3 × 3 = 9, so the bottom line is × 3 too: 240 × 3 = 720 g.
Card 2 (practice values): 1 kg of rice costs ₹36. What do 4 kg 500 g cost? Answer: 4 kg cost 4 × 36 = ₹144, 500 g is half of 1,000 g so it costs 36 ÷ 2 = ₹18, and 144 + 18 = ₹162.
Card 3 (practice values): 6 kg cost ₹90. What does 1 kg cost? Answer: the top line goes ÷ 6 from 6 kg to 1 kg, so the bottom line goes ÷ 6 too: 90 ÷ 6 = ₹15.

Card 4 (practice values): press Try adding instead on the 3 plates and 240 g line, adding 6 to both. What do you see? Answer: 9 plates but 246 g, which is far less than 720 g, so adding does not keep the lines in step; multiply both.
Challenge: '4 people need 500 g rice for a meal. How much rice will be needed for 8 people if they eat similar quantity of rice?' Answer: 4 to 8 is × 2, so 500 × 2 = 1,000 g, which is 1 kg.
Challenge: '5 kg of tomatoes cost ₹73. How much will 10 kg of tomatoes cost?' Answer: 5 to 10 is × 2, so 73 × 2 = ₹146.

Challenge: 'Nitesh is a scrap dealer. How much would he have paid for (a) 16 kg of old newspaper, if he paid ₹8 for every 1 kg of newspaper? (b) 20 kg iron, if he paid ₹200 for every 10 kg of iron? (c) 10 kg plastic, if he paid ₹30 for 5 kg of plastic? Make double number lines for answering (b) and (c).' Answer: (a) 16 × 8 = ₹128; (b) 10 to 20 is × 2, 200 × 2 = ₹400; (c) 5 to 10 is × 2, 30 × 2 = ₹60.

tool_questions: Card 1 (practice values): 3 plates need 240 g of lentils. How many grams do 9 plates need? Answer: the top line is × 3 because 3 × 3 = 9, so the bottom line is × 3 too: 240 × 3 = 720 g.
Card 2 (practice values): 1 kg of rice costs ₹36. What do 4 kg 500 g cost? Answer: 4 kg cost 4 × 36 = ₹144, 500 g is half of 1,000 g so it costs 36 ÷ 2 = ₹18, and 144 + 18 = ₹162.
Card 3 (practice values): 6 kg cost ₹90. What does 1 kg cost? Answer: the top line goes ÷ 6 from 6 kg to 1 kg, so the bottom line goes ÷ 6 too: 90 ÷ 6 = ₹15.

Card 4 (practice values): press Try adding instead on the 3 plates and 240 g line, adding 6 to both. What do you see? Answer: 9 plates but 246 g, which is far less than 720 g, so adding does not keep the lines in step; multiply both.
Challenge: '4 people need 500 g rice for a meal. How much rice will be needed for 8 people if they eat similar quantity of rice?' Answer: 4 to 8 is × 2, so 500 × 2 = 1,000 g, which is 1 kg.
Challenge: '5 kg of tomatoes cost ₹73. How much will 10 kg of tomatoes cost?' Answer: 5 to 10 is × 2, so 73 × 2 = ₹146.

Challenge: 'Nitesh is a scrap dealer. How much would he have paid for (a) 16 kg of old newspaper, if he paid ₹8 for every 1 kg of newspaper? (b) 20 kg iron, if he paid ₹200 for every 10 kg of iron? (c) 10 kg plastic, if he paid ₹30 for 5 kg of plastic? Make double number lines for answering (b) and (c).' Answer: (a) 16 × 8 = ₹128; (b) 10 to 20 is × 2, 200 × 2 = ₹400; (c) 5 to 10 is × 2, 30 × 2 = ₹60.

Worked example: Rice costs ₹36 for 1 kg. What is the cost of 4 kg 500 g of rice? These are practice values.
1. Split the weight: 4 kg 500 g is 4 kg and 500 g.
2. The cost of 4 kg: 4 × 36 = ₹144.
3. 500 g is half of 1,000 g, so it costs half of ₹36: 36 ÷ 2 = ₹18.
4. Add: 144 + 18 = ₹162.
5. Check: 4 kg 500 g is more than 4 kg and less than 5 kg. 4 kg costs ₹144 and 5 kg costs 5 × 36 = ₹180, and ₹162 is between them.
Answer: 4 kg 500 g of rice costs ₹162

content.text:
1. Predict first: 3 plates need 240 g of lentils. For 9 plates, do you add 6 to the 240 g, or multiply it?
2. Look at the top line: 3 plates to 9 plates is × 3, because 3 × 3 = 9.
3. A double number line keeps two quantities in step. Whatever you do to the top number, you do the same to the bottom number.
4. So the bottom line is also × 3: 240 × 3 = 720 g.
5. Adding the same number to both lines does not work. 3 + 6 = 9 plates, but 240 + 6 = 246 g is far too little for 9 plates.
6. To go down, divide both lines by the same number.
7. Rule: find what the first line was multiplied by, then multiply the second line by the same number.

media.teaching_notes: 1. The total cost is the cost of 1 kg times the weight. Split each weight into whole kg and a part of a kg. 2. Rice, 12 kg 500 g at ₹60: 12 × 60 = ₹720. 500 g is half of 1,000 g, so it costs 60 ÷ 2 = ₹30. 720 + 30 = ₹750. 3. Flour, 7 kg 250 g at ₹40: 7 × 40 = ₹280. 250 g is a quarter of 1,000 g, so it costs 40 ÷ 4 = ₹10. 280 + 10 = ₹290. 4. Sugar, 5 kg at ₹45: 5 × 45 = ₹225. 5. Chana dal, 3 kg 600 g at ₹70: 3 × 70 = ₹210. 100 g is a tenth of 1,000 g, so 100 g costs 70 ÷ 10 = ₹7 and 600 g costs 6 × 7 = ₹42. 210 + 42 = ₹252. 6. Besan, 4 kg at ₹60: 4 × 60 = ₹240. 7. Jaggery, 1 kg 400 g at ₹50: 1 × 50 = ₹50. 100 g costs 50 ÷ 10 = ₹5 and 400 g costs 4 × 5 = ₹20. 50 + 20 = ₹70. 8. Check: ₹750 for the rice is more than 12 kg at ₹720 and less than 13 kg at 13 × 60 = ₹780. Answer: Rice: ₹750; Flour: ₹290; Sugar: ₹225; Chana dal: ₹252; Besan: ₹240; Jaggery: ₹70

content.question_tex: The cost of some grocery items is given in the following table. Find the total cost of each item. Rice: $12\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$, cost of $1\text{ kg}$ ₹$60$. Flour: $7\text{ kg}\; 250\text{ g}$, ₹$40$. Sugar: $5\text{ kg}$, ₹$45$. Chana dal: $3\text{ kg}\; 600\text{ g}$, ₹$70$. Besan: $4\text{ kg}$, ₹$60$. Jaggery: $1\text{ kg}\; 400\text{ g}$, ₹$50$.
content.publication_text: The cost of some grocery items is given in the following table. Find the total cost of each item. Rice: $12\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$, cost of $1\text{ kg}$ ₹$60$. Flour: $7\text{ kg}\; 250\text{ g}$, ₹$40$. Sugar: $5\text{ kg}$, ₹$45$. Chana dal: $3\text{ kg}\; 600\text{ g}$, ₹$70$. Besan: $4\text{ kg}$, ₹$60$. Jaggery: $1\text{ kg}\; 400\text{ g}$, ₹$50$.

content.text:
1. The total cost is the cost of $1\text{ kg}$ times the weight. Split each weight into whole kilograms and a part of a kilogram.
2. Rice, $12\text{ kg}\; 500\text{ g}$ at ₹$60$: $12 \times 60 =$ ₹$720$. $500\text{ g}$ is half of $1,000\text{ g}$, so it costs $60 \div 2 =$ ₹$30$. $720 + 30 =$ ₹$750$.
3. Flour, $7\text{ kg}\; 250\text{ g}$ at ₹$40$: $7 \times 40 =$ ₹$280$. $250\text{ g}$ is a quarter of $1,000\text{ g}$, so it costs $40 \div 4 =$ ₹$10$. $280 + 10 =$ ₹$290$.
4. Sugar, $5\text{ kg}$ at ₹$45$: $5 \times 45 =$ ₹$225$.
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution]
5. Chana dal, $3\text{ kg}\; 600\text{ g}$ at ₹$70$: $3 \times 70 =$ ₹$210$. $100\text{ g}$ is a tenth of $1,000\text{ g}$, so $100\text{ g}$ costs $70 \div 10 =$ ₹$7$ and $600\text{ g}$ costs $6 \times 7 =$ ₹$42$. $210 + 42 =$ ₹$252$.
6. Besan, $4\text{ kg}$ at ₹$60$: $4 \times 60 =$ ₹$240$.
7. Jaggery, $1\text{ kg}\; 400\text{ g}$ at ₹$50$: $1 \times 50 =$ ₹$50$. $100\text{ g}$ costs $50 \div 10 =$ ₹$5$ and $400\text{ g}$ costs $4 \times 5 =$ ₹$20$. $50 + 20 =$ ₹$70$.
8. Check: ₹$750$ for the rice is more than $12\text{ kg}$ at ₹$720$ and less than $13\text{ kg}$ at $13 \times 60 =$ ₹$780$.
Answer: Rice: ₹$750$; Flour: ₹$290$; Sugar: ₹$225$; Chana dal: ₹$252$; Besan: ₹$240$; Jaggery: ₹$70$
[Image: Let us do: Ans1: solution (continued)]

Chana dal, 3 kg 600 g at ₹70: 3 × 70 = ₹210. 100 g is a tenth of 1,000 g, so 100 g costs 70 ÷ 10 = ₹7 and 600 g costs 6 × 7 = ₹42. 210 + 42 = ₹252.

content.publication_text: You must have seen tea being prepared at your home. How much water and milk do we need to make $2$ cups of tea? Do we need $1\text{ l}$ of water to make $2$ cups of tea? Is $500\text{ ml}$ of water enough for $2$ cups of tea?

content.text:
1. A cup is small, so two cups need only a small amount of water and milk.
2. $1\text{ l}$ is $1,000\text{ ml}$. That is far more than two cups need, so we do not need $1\text{ l}$ of water.
3. Take a cup of about $150\text{ ml} ($a practice value; cups are not all the same). Two cups hold $2 \times 150 = 300\text{ ml}$.
4. For example, $200\text{ ml}$ of water and $100\text{ ml}$ of milk make $200 + 100 = 300\text{ ml}$.
5. $300\text{ ml}$ is less than $500\text{ ml}$, so $500\text{ ml}$ of water is enough for $2$ cups, and it is more than enough.
6. Check: $300\text{ ml}$ is less than $500\text{ ml}$, and $500\text{ ml}$ is less than $1,000\text{ ml}$.
Answer: Sample answer: about $300\text{ ml}$ in all $(200\text{ ml}$ of water, $100\text{ ml}$ of milk). No, $1\text{ l}$ is not needed. Yes, $500\text{ ml}$ is enough. Your answer may differ.

content.text: A bucket can hold a maximum of $20\text{ ml}$ of water. Is this statement correct? Which unit should be used in such a situation?
content.question: A bucket can hold a maximum of 20 ml of water. Is this statement correct? Which unit should be used in such a situation?
content.book_number: Measuring Capacity: the bucket
content.question_tex: A bucket can hold a maximum of $20\text{ ml}$ of water. Is this statement correct? Which unit should be used in such a situation?
content.publication_text: A bucket can hold a maximum of $20\text{ ml}$ of water. Is this statement correct? Which unit should be used in such a situation?

content.text:
1. $20\text{ ml}$ is a very small amount, and a bucket holds much more than that.
2. A water bottle of $500\text{ ml}$ holds $25$ times as much as $20\text{ ml}$, because $500 \div 20 = 25$.
3. A bucket holds much more than a water bottle, so it cannot hold at most $20\text{ ml}$. The statement is not correct.
4. A bucket holds a big amount, so the unit to use is the litre, $l$.
5. Check: for example, a bucket of $10\text{ l}$ holds $10 \times 1,000 = 10,000\text{ ml}$, which is much more than $20\text{ ml}$.
Answer: No, the statement is not correct. A bucket should be measured in litres.
